paragraphs.text: Exhortation to the Heathen (Chapter 7)
BY CLEMENT OF ALEXANDRIA
Chapter 7. The Poets Also Bear Testimony to the Truth.

Let poetry also approach to us (for philosophy alone will not suffice): poetry which is wholly occupied with falsehood— which scarcely will make confession of the truth, but will rather own to God its deviations into fable. Let whoever of those poets chooses advance first. Aratus considers that the power of God pervades all things:—

<quote>That all may be secure,
Him ever they propitiate first and last,
Hail, Father I great marvel, great gain to man.</quote>
Thus also the Ascræan Hesiod dimly speaks of God:—

<quote>For He is the King of all, and monarch
Of the immortals; and there is none that may vie
with Him in power.</quote>
Also on the stage they reveal the truth:—
<quote>Look on the ether and heaven, and regard that as God,</quote>
says Euripides. And Sophocles, the son of Sophilus, says:—

<quote>One, in truth, one is God,
Who made both heaven and the far-stretching earth,
And ocean's blue wave, and the mighty winds;
But many of us mortals, deceived in heart,
Have set up for ourselves, as a consolation in our afflictions,
Images of the gods of stone, or wood, or brass,
Or gold, or ivory;
And, appointing to those sacrifices and vain festal assemblages,
Are accustomed thus to practice religion.</quote>

In this venturous manner has he on the stage brought truth before the spectators. But the Thracian Orpheus, the son of Œagrus, hierophant and poet at once, after his exposition of the orgies, and his theology of idols, introduces a palinode of truth with true solemnity, though tardily singing the strain:—

I shall utter to whom it is lawful; but let the doors be closed, Nevertheless, against all the profane. But do you hear, O Musæus, offspring of the light-bringing moon, For I will declare what is true. And let not these things Which once appeared in your breast rob you of dear life; But looking to the divine word, apply yourself to it, Keeping right the seat of intellect and feeling; and walk well In the straight path, and to the immortal King of the universe alone Direct your gaze.
Then proceeding, he clearly adds:—

<quote>He is one, self-proceeding; and from Him alone all things proceed,
And in them He Himself exerts his activity: no mortal
Beholds Him, but He beholds all.</quote>
Thus far Orpheus at last understood that he had been in error:—

<quote>But linger no longer, O man, endued with varied wisdom;
But turn and retrace your steps, and propitiate God.</quote>

For if, at the most, the Greeks, having received certain scintillations of the divine word, have given forth some utterances of truth, they bear indeed witness that the force of truth is not hidden, and at the same time expose their own weakness in not having arrived at the end. For I think it has now become evident to all, that those who do or speak anything without the word of truth are like people compelled to walk without feet. Let the strictures on your gods, which the poets, impelled by the force of truth, introduce in their comedies, shame you into salvation. Menander, for instance, the comic poet, in his drama of the Charioteer, says:—

<quote>No God pleases me that goes about
With an old woman, and enters houses
Carrying a trencher.</quote>
For such are the begging priests of Cybele. Hence Antisthenes replies appropriately to their request for alms:—

<quote>I do not maintain the mother of the gods,
For the gods maintain her.</quote>

Again, the same writer of comedy, expressing his dissatisfaction with the common usages, tries to expose the impious arrogance of the prevailing error in the drama of the Priestess, sagely declaring:—

<quote>If a man drags the Deity
Whither he will by the sound of cymbals,
He that does this is greater than the Deity;
But these are the instruments of audacity and means of living
Invented by men.</quote>

And not only Menander, but Homer also, and Euripides, and other poets in great numbers, expose your gods, and are wont to rate them, and that soundly too. For instance, they call Aphrodite dog-fly, and Hephæstus a cripple. Helen says to Aphrodite:—

<quote>Your godship abdicate!
Renounce Olympus!</quote>
And of Dionysus, Homer writes without reserve:—

<quote>He, mid their frantic orgies, in the groves
Of lovely Nyssa, put to shameful rout
The youthful Bacchus' nurses; they in fear,
Dropped each her thyrsus, scattered by the hand
Of fierce Lycurgus, with an ox-goad armed.</quote>
Worthy truly of the Socratic school is Euripides, who fixes his eye on truth, and despises the spectators of his plays. On one occasion, Apollo,

<quote>Who inhabits the sanctuary that is in the middle of the earth,
Dispensing most certain oracles to mortals,</quote>
is thus exposed:—

<quote>It was in obedience to him that I killed her who brought me forth;
Him do you regard as stained with guilt— put him to death;
It was he that sinned, not I, uninstructed as I was
In right and justice.</quote>

He introduces Heracles, at one time mad, at another drunk and gluttonous. How should he not so represent the god who, when entertained as a guest, ate green figs to flesh, uttering discordant howls, that even his barbarian host remarked it? In his drama of Ion, too, he barefacedly brings the gods on the stage:—

<quote>How, then, is it right for you, who have given laws to mortals,
To be yourselves guilty of wrong?
And if— what will never take place, yet I will state the supposition—
You will give satisfaction to men for your adulteries,
You, Poseidon, and you, Zeus, the ruler of heaven,—
You will, in order to make recompense for your misdeeds,
Have to empty your temples.</quote>

latex.p0003: 第七章　诗人们也为真理作证
latex.p0004: 让诗歌也来接近我们（因为仅凭哲学是不够的）；诗歌虽全然充斥着虚假，却几乎不愿承认真理，反倒会向天主承认自己偏离到神话中。让那些诗人中任何一位首先上前吧。\newline{}\Person{阿拉托斯}认为天主的权能渗透万有：——
latex.p0005: \Quote{为使一切安稳，\newline{}他们始终首先并最后祈求祂，\newline{}万福，圣父啊！伟大的奇迹，对人的巨大恩赐。}
latex.p0006: 同样，阿斯克拉的\Person{赫西俄德}也隐约谈及天主：——
latex.p0007: \Quote{因为祂是万有的君王，\newline{}不死者的主宰；没有谁能\newline{}与祂的权能抗衡。}
latex.p0008: 在舞台上，他们也揭示真理：——
latex.p0010: ——\Person{欧里庇得斯}说。而\Person{索福克勒斯}，\Person{索菲洛斯}之子，说：——
latex.p0011:
\Quote{一，确实，仅有一位天主，
ewline{}祂造了天和广袤的地，
ewline{}以及海洋的碧波和强劲的风；
ewline{}但我们许多有死之人，心受蒙蔽，
ewline{}为自己立起了——作为逆境中的慰藉——
ewline{}石头、木头、青铜、
ewline{}黄金或象牙所造的神像；
ewline{}并为那些神像献祭和举行徒然的节庆集会，
ewline{}习惯于如此实践宗教。}
latex.p0012: 他就这样大胆地在舞台上将真理摆在观众面前。但色雷斯人\Person{俄耳甫斯}，\Person{俄阿格洛斯}之子，既是秘仪祭司又是诗人，在描述秘仪和偶像神学之后，以真正的庄严引入了真理的翻案诗，虽然姗姗来迟地唱道：——
latex.p0013:
\Quote{我将向那些蒙允许的人宣说；但要关上门，
ewline{}无论如何，反对一切不敬者。但你听，
ewline{}哦\Person{穆赛俄斯}，光明的月亮所生之子，
ewline{}因为我要宣告何为真实。不要让这些
ewline{}曾出现在你胸中的事物夺去你宝贵的生命；
ewline{}但要仰望神圣的言语，专注于它，
ewline{}保持\Emph{理智和情感的座位}正直，并行走在
ewline{}笔直的道路上，只向宇宙的不朽君王
ewline{}定睛注视。}
latex.p0015: \Quote{祂是独一的，自存的；万物从祂独一而来，\newline{}祂自身在万物中活动：没有凡人\newline{}看见祂，但祂看见万有。}
latex.p0016: 至此\Person{俄耳甫斯}终于明白自己犯了错误：——
latex.p0017: \Quote{但不要再犹豫了，哦，富有多种智慧的人；\newline{}回转吧，退返你的脚步，求悦于天主。}
latex.p0018: 因为，最多而言，希腊人领受了神圣言语的些许火花，发出了某些真实的话语；他们确实见证真理的力量并不隐藏，同时也暴露了自己的软弱——未能抵达终点。因为我认为现在对所有人已经清楚：那些没有真理之言而行事或说话的人，就像被迫无脚行走之人。愿诗人们因真理之力而在喜剧中引入的对你们诸神的斥责，使你们羞愧而得到救恩。例如，喜剧诗人\Person{米南德}在他的剧作\WorkTitle{驭手}中说：——
latex.p0019: \Quote{没有一个神令我喜悦，他\newline{}跟着一个老妇人，进入房屋，\newline{}端着一个盘子。}
latex.p0020: 因为\Person{库柏勒}的乞讨祭司就是如此。因此\Person{安提斯泰尼}对他们的乞讨作了恰当的回答：——
latex.p0021: \Quote{我不供养众神之母，\newline{}因为众神供养她。}
latex.p0022: 同样，那位喜剧作家不满意通常的习俗，试图在剧作\WorkTitle{女祭司}中揭露流行错误的邪恶傲慢，明智地宣告：——
latex.p0023:
\Quote{如果一个人用手鼓的响声
ewline{}将神祇随意拖曳，
ewline{}做此事的人就比神祇更大；
ewline{}但这些乃是狂妄的工具和谋生的手段，
ewline{}由人发明。}
latex.p0024: 不仅\Person{米南德}，而且\Person{荷马}、\Person{欧里庇得斯}以及其他大量诗人，都揭露你们的诸神，并惯于斥责他们，而且斥责得相当厉害。例如，他们称\Person{阿佛洛狄忒}为狗蝇，称\Person{赫淮斯托斯}为瘸子。\Person{海伦}对\Person{阿佛洛狄忒}说：——
latex.p0025: \Quote{你的神位退位吧！\newline{}放弃奥林波斯！}
latex.p0026: 关于\Person{狄俄尼索斯}，\Person{荷马}毫无保留地写道：——
latex.p0027:
\Quote{他在可爱的\Place{倪萨}的树林中，
ewline{}{在}他们的狂欢秘仪里，
ewline{}使年轻的\Person{巴科斯}的乳母们狼狈溃逃；
ewline{}她们恐惧，
ewline{}各自丢弃了神杖，被凶猛的\Person{吕枯尔戈斯}手持刺棒驱散。}
latex.p0028: 真正配得上苏格拉底学派的是\Person{欧里庇得斯}，他注目真理，藐视看戏的观众。有一次，\Person{阿波罗}，
latex.p0029: \Quote{祂居住在大地中央的圣所，\newline{}向凡人所发最确切的神谕，}
latex.p0031:
\Quote{我服从他杀了生我的她；
ewline{}你视他为有罪——将他处死；
ewline{}是他犯了罪，而不是我，因为我未受教导
ewline{}{关于}正义与公平。}
latex.p0032: 他引入\Person{赫拉克勒斯}时而疯狂，时而醉酒贪食。他岂能不如此描绘那位神祇？当神祇被招待为客时，他大嚼生绿无花果，发出刺耳的嚎叫，甚至连他那蛮族的东道主都注意到了。在他的剧作\WorkTitle{伊昂}中，他也厚颜无耻地将诸神搬上舞台：——
latex.p0033:
\Quote{那么，你们这些为凡人立法者，
ewline{}自己却行不义，这如何合理？
ewline{}如果——这绝不会发生，但我仍如此假设——
ewline{}你们要向人交出你们通奸的帐，
ewline{}你，\Person{波塞冬}，还有你，\Person{宙斯}，天界的统治者，——
ewline{}你们将为了补偿你们的恶行
ewline{}不得不腾空你们的圣殿。}
